items.title: What do employers usually look at in hiring?

values: Complete fictional inputs

A fictional 16-week undergraduate course "Introduction to Cross-Cultural and Area Studies" at Minghu University, 90 minutes per week, with 60 students of whom 20 are from other majors. Three objectives: explain evidence and opinion, cite properly, and avoid generalizing a single case to a whole group. Assessment is proposed as 20% class participation, 30% short papers, 20% group presentation, and 30% final case, totaling 100%.

Fictional reference S1: Lin Cheng, Bridge Bay Festival Records, 2024, page 12: "Of the 10 households surveyed at Bridge Bay, 6 took part in the community festival. The participation rate for the whole city cannot be inferred from these 10 households." S2: Zhou Ye, Urban Mutual Aid Cases, 2023, page 8: "Interviews in Community A found that respondents linked neighborhood mutual aid with work arrangements." Both texts are invented for practice and are not real literature.

Five excerpts to assess: A "Of the 10 households surveyed at Bridge Bay, 6 took part in the community festival." no quotation marks and no source; B "60% of the whole city took part in the festival (Lin Cheng, 2024, page 12)"; C "All mutual aid among Community A residents is determined by work arrangements (Zhou Ye, 2023)"; D "Zhou Ye points out that respondents in Community A linked mutual aid with work arrangements (Lin Cheng, 2024, page 12)"; E "Interviews in Community A found that respondents linked neighborhood mutual aid with work arrangements." (Zhou Ye, 2023) with quotation marks and author-year but no page. The given practice scoring has five items of 20 each: faithfulness to the limited scope, distinguishing quotation from paraphrase, author-year match, locating the page, and identifying limitations; no real students are assessed.

Fictional research materials R1: the Bridge Bay 2024 record of festival participation for ten households only counts whether they took part and did not collect reasons; R2: the Community A 2023 five interviews only concern mutual aid and work arrangements, not the same area or topic. The research idea is the reasons for festival participation at Bridge Bay, proposing to recruit 12 volunteer adults for interviews, without investigating real people; the funding exercise requires a two-page abstract of up to 250 characters per page.
Three deliverable tasks
Task one: give the 16-week course schedule and the week 4 90-minute activity, with the three objectives mapped to assessment; provide concept explanations for students from other majors.

Task two: assess the specific problems in A—E one by one, score them on the given five items, and write revised text and course prevention; score only the citation and evidence quality of the excerpts, not a whole paper grade.

Task three: write a two-page research abstract per R1/R2, covering the problem, known gap, interview method, ethics, contribution, and limitations; do not treat fictional materials or future results as real findings.
Complete reference deliverables

Course reference: 1—2 concepts and evidence, 3—4 source citation, 5—6 regional cases and scope, 7—8 ethnic identity, 9—10 gender and cross-cultural perspectives, 11—12 research questions and interview ethics, 13—14 group cases, 15 review, 16 final case. Objective 1 uses short papers and cases, objective 2 uses citation exercises and papers, objective 3 uses group presentations and cases; weights 20+30+20+30=100. Week 4 runs 10+15+20+20+15+10=90 minutes (concept review, citation demonstration, small-group check, feedback, revision, exit slip); 10 groups of 6 with 2 non-majors.

Scoring reference: A faithful scope 20, distinguishing quotation 0, author-year 0, page 0, limitations 0 = 20; B scope 0, paraphrase 20, author-year 20, page 20, limitations 0 = 60; C scope 0, paraphrase 20, author-year 20, page 0, limitations 0 = 40; D scope 20, paraphrase 20, author-year 0, page 0, limitations 0 = 40; E scope 20, quotation 20, author-year 20, page 0, limitations 0 = 60. Any excerpt without a limitation statement scores 0, and D still does not match the correct S2 location even though page 12 is written.

Revision reference: A adds quotation marks and (Lin Cheng, 2024, page 12) and notes that it covers only 10 households; B is changed to 6 of the 10 households in the Bridge Bay survey, which cannot be generalized to the whole city; C is changed to respondents in Community A linking mutual aid with work arrangements, not everyone or causality, with page 8 added; D is changed to (Zhou Ye, 2023, page 8) and notes the limitations of the Community A interviews; E adds page 8 and notes it covers only the interview material. Prevention: provide citation examples, an author and page checklist, and case scope labels, self-check before submission, and do not judge plagiarism automatically from a similarity score.

Abstract page 1 reference: the research asks how Bridge Bay adults explain festival participation. R1 has only the participation record for 10 households and no reasons; R2 is an interview about mutual aid elsewhere and cannot explain the Bridge Bay festival. The plan is to recruit 12 adults voluntarily for semi-structured interviews, record views by participation and non-participation, code themes anonymously, and keep the analysis steps. This gap is derived only from the given fictional materials and does not claim a real literature gap. Page 2 reference: first verify the ethics procedures as required by the institution and explain voluntary withdrawal, recording consent, de-identification, and restricted access, without investigating real people. The expected outputs are an anonymous theme comparison and a methods reflection, and it cannot be announced in advance that the reasons for participation are confirmed; the small self-selected and non-random sample cannot estimate the citywide proportion, prove causality, or represent all ethnic groups. Each page is up to 250 characters, and the exercise cannot serve as real research results.

The prompt sources, assignments, and research are all fictional, contain no real institutional student or respondent data, and no recruitment or interviewing is carried out.

subject.name: Area, Ethnic, and Cultural Studies Teachers, Postsecondary
subject.summary: Area, ethnic, and cultural studies teachers at colleges and universities teach courses on the culture and development of regions, ethnic groups, or other groups, such as Latin American studies, women's studies, and urban affairs, including both teaching-focused and teaching-and-research positions. Tasks include leading discussions, lecturing, preparing lessons, grading examinations and assignments, keeping up with the discipline, revising courses, conducting and publishing research, holding question sessions, keeping grades and attendance, collaborating, advising students, applying for funding, and departmental and community service. The US BLS typical entry-level education is a doctoral or professional degree; O*NET is Job Zone Five, SVP8+, and 61% of respondents answered that newly hired personnel need a doctorate, 31% a master's, and 4% postdoctoral training. These are answers about education requirements, not the nationwide educational composition of incumbents or a uniform Chinese threshold. Chinese qualification, position, and appointment follow the Higher Education Law and actual announcements, and Chinese and US statistics are kept separate.
